Guide.Article.welcome.Title: Welcome
Guide.Article.welcome.Summary: Learn what the level editor can do and where to begin.
Guide.Article.welcome.Intro: Cut the Rope DX: Level Editor creates and edits levels for Cut the Rope: DX. Use the **palette** to add objects, the **canvas** to arrange them, and the **inspector** to organize layers and edit exact values.
Guide.Article.welcome.Route.Heading: A good first route
Guide.Article.welcome.Route.Steps:
Create a level and choose its size, mechanics, and background.
Drag Om Nom, candy, a rope hook, and stars from the palette.
Arrange the objects on the canvas, then save the level.
Use **File > Play This Level** to try it in Cut the Rope: DX.
Guide.Article.welcome.Layout.Caption: The editor with the palette, canvas, layers, and properties labelled.
Guide.Article.welcome.Search.Tip: You can open this guide while editing and use search to jump directly to an object or shortcut.
Guide.Article.first-level.Title: Create your first level
Guide.Article.first-level.Summary: Build a small playable level from an empty document.
Guide.Article.first-level.Build.Steps:
Choose **File > New**, pick a resolution, and set the mechanics and background.
Drag Om Nom and a candy from the palette onto the canvas.
Add a rope hook above the candy; with a single candy it binds automatically.
Add one to three stars along the path the candy will swing through.
Choose **File > Save As**, then **File > Play This Level** to try it in the game.
Guide.Article.first-level.Validation.Not: The validator warns when essential objects or bindings are missing. You may still save, edit, or playtest after reviewing the warning.
Guide.Article.first-level.Example.Captio: A simple level with Om Nom, candy, a rope, and three stars.
Guide.Article.know-the-editor.Title: Know the editor
Guide.Article.know-the-editor.Summary: Identify the palette, canvas, layers, properties, and compact controls.
Guide.Article.know-the-editor.Expanded: The **palette** is on the left, the **level canvas** is in the center, and **Layers** and **Properties** share the inspector on the right. **File**, **Edit**, **View**, and **Help** commands appear in the menu bar.
Guide.Article.know-the-editor.Compact: On a narrow window, the canvas takes priority. **Palette** and **Layers** move behind bottom tabs, contextual editing actions appear near the selection, and the **hamburger drawer** contains the remaining commands.
Guide.Article.know-the-editor.Layouts.Ca: Expanded and compact editor layouts side by side.
Guide.Article.add-place-objects.Title: Add and place objects
Guide.Article.add-place-objects.Summary: Find objects in the palette and place them on the canvas.
Guide.Article.add-place-objects.Place.St:
Use the palette search box, or expand the Cut the Rope or Cut the Rope: Experiments group.
Drag an available object from the palette onto the level.
Drag the placed object to reposition it; grid snapping applies when it is on.
Use Properties when an exact coordinate or an object-specific value is required.
Guide.Article.add-place-objects.Availabi: Objects that do not suit the current level are hidden in the palette: plain candy while Half candy is on, and the left and right halves while it is off. Objects that differ only by a size or an icon appear once in the palette, with the variant chosen in Properties afterwards.
Guide.Article.add-place-objects.Drag.Cap: Dragging an object from the palette to the canvas.
Guide.Article.select-transform.Title: Select and transform objects
Guide.Article.select-transform.Summary: Select one or many objects, move them, rotate them, and use contextual handles.
Guide.Article.select-transform.Selection: Click an object to select it. **Ctrl-click** or **Command-click** adds or removes an object from the selection, and either modifier works on *any platform*. Drag any member of a selection to move the whole group together.
Guide.Article.select-transform.Handles: A selected object shows only the handles it supports: a **rotation dial**, a **radius ring**, resize grips, a rail, path points, or mechanical-hand bones and joints. An object with nothing to adjust shows none.
Guide.Article.select-transform.Duplicate: Ctrl-drag or Command-drag an already selected object past the drag threshold to duplicate the selection and move the copy. Below that threshold the gesture is still treated as a click, so a slightly unsteady hand will not leave stray copies.
Guide.Article.select-transform.RotationS: Rotation dials snap in 15-degree steps. Hold Alt during a drag to snap just that drag, or latch it with **Edit > Snap Rotation**.
Guide.Article.select-transform.Handles.C: Common selection, rotation, resize, and radius handles.
Guide.Article.clipboard-lock-hide.Title: Copy, paste, lock, hide, and delete
Guide.Article.clipboard-lock-hide.Summar: Reuse objects and protect parts of a level from accidental edits.
Guide.Article.clipboard-lock-hide.Clipbo: Use **Edit > Cut**, **Copy**, **Paste**, **Select All**, and **Delete**, or their keyboard shortcuts. **Select All** targets the active layer rather than the whole level. **Ctrl-drag** or **Command-drag** is a faster way to duplicate objects in place. **Copy** also puts the selected objects on the system clipboard as XML, ready to paste into a level file or a message. **Paste** only ever places what was copied inside the editor.
Guide.Article.clipboard-lock-hide.Lockin: The **Layers** tree has a visibility and a lock button on every layer and object row. Double-clicking an object on the canvas locks or unlocks it too. A *locked* object takes every canvas click until it is unlocked, which is what makes it useful as a background you cannot disturb.
Guide.Article.clipboard-lock-hide.Delete: Deleting a layer also removes every object inside it. The confirmation explains the scope, and the operation can be undone.
Guide.Article.layers.Title: Work with layers
Guide.Article.layers.Summary: Organize object drawing order and lock or hide groups of objects.
Guide.Article.layers.Intro: **Layers** control organization and drawing order. Use the controls beneath the tree to add, delete, move, or merge layers.
Guide.Article.layers.Organize.Steps:
Select a layer to make it active.
Rename it from the row action when a descriptive name is useful.
Drag rows to reorder layers or objects.
Use the eye and lock buttons to hide or protect a whole layer or one object.
Guide.Article.layers.InheritedState.Note: Locked or hidden parent layers affect their objects even when an individual object row appears enabled.
Guide.Article.layers.Panel.Caption: The Layers panel and its row actions.
Guide.Article.edit-properties.Title: Edit properties
Guide.Article.edit-properties.Summary: Adjust exact coordinates and object-specific behavior in the inspector.
Guide.Article.edit-properties.Fields: Select an object to show its fields in **Properties**: position, rotation, size, bindings, movement, and whatever gameplay values that object supports. Some fields appear only once a related one is switched *on*, so the panel changes shape as you edit.
Guide.Article.edit-properties.Help: Fields whose meaning is not obvious carry an **inline help** button explaining what the value does and what its default means. A field the game cannot combine with the object's current state is greyed out rather than hidden, so the panel does not jump around. Attributes this editor does not recognize are preserved untouched when the level is saved.
Canvas handles and property fields edit the same data. Use the canvas for visual placement and Properties for exact values.
Guide.Article.level-settings.Title: Configure level settings
Guide.Article.level-settings.Summary: Choose the level's name, dimensions, mechanics, gravity, water, and visual customization.
Guide.Article.level-settings.Name: **Level name** is the name the game shows for the level, and the one it reports to Discord rich presence. Leave it empty for an unnamed level. The game looks the text up in its own string table first, which is how the shipped packs store a translation key there; anything it does not recognize is shown exactly as you typed it. A named level also seeds the file name the first time you save it or take a screenshot, with any character a file name cannot hold replaced by an underscore; once the level has a file, that file's name is what saving suggests.
Guide.Article.level-settings.Mechanics: **Edit > Level Settings** sets the resolution, the rope physics speed, and the special tutorial prompt. **Half candy** splits the goal into a left and a right half, as in Valentine's Box. **Night level** darkens the stage so only light bulbs reveal the stars, as in Pillow Box.
Guide.Article.level-settings.Gravity: **Gravity** is the pull applied to everything in the level. **Vertical** is *784* for normal gravity, *0* for a weightless level, and negative to pull upward; **Horizontal** is *0* by default and pushes to the right when positive. Both are left out of the saved file while they hold those defaults, so only a level that actually changes gravity carries them.
Guide.Article.level-settings.Water: **Water height** is the depth of the pool pinned to the bottom of the level; *0* means no water. **Water drain speed** is how fast that pool empties during play, in level units per second; *0* keeps it static. The dialog shows how long a non-zero speed takes to drain the pool.
Guide.Article.level-settings.Physics: **Use mobile physics** writes *useMobilePhysics* into the level's *gameDesign* and selects the mobile collision model. Several objects, including candy, stars, spikes, bouncers, and the snail, have different collision boxes under the two models, so **View > Show Hitboxes** changes with this setting.
Guide.Article.level-settings.Customizati: The same dialog configures rope color, background, candy skin, and Om Nom's platform. Tick **Remember my customization choices** to reuse them for new levels.
Guide.Article.level-settings.Palette.Not: Changing a mechanic changes which palette objects are valid. Half candy hides plain candy and enables the left and right halves; turning it off does the reverse. A night level without a light bulb is reported by validation.
Guide.Article.level-settings.Dialog.Capt: Level Settings with mechanics and customization sections.
Guide.Article.objectives.Title: Om Nom and candy
Guide.Article.objectives.Summary: The two objects every level needs, Om Nom's skin, and how candy is numbered.
Guide.Article.objectives.SearchTerms: om nom|candy|target|goal|half candy|candyL|candyR|candy number|om nom skin|targetType
Guide.Article.objectives.InGame: The goal of every level is to get the candy into Om Nom's mouth. Om Nom sits still and waits; the candy is the only object the player is really moving. Touching Om Nom's mouth wins the level immediately, whatever else is still on screen.
Guide.Article.objectives.InGameNightMode: In night mode, light bulb acts as secondary objective that player must guide it to wake Om Nom up. Without it, the level loses.
Guide.Article.objectives.Editing: Drag Om Nom and a candy from the palette. Candy has no properties of its own, so position is the entire design decision, and Om Nom adds only a skin. Om Nom's collision box is a thin strip at his mouth rather than his whole body, so use **View > Show Hitboxes** when placing him close to other objects.
Guide.Article.objectives.Skin: **Om Nom skin** picks the look in this level, from the classic sprite through the seasonal and costume skins. **Player's choice**, the default, leaves him as whatever skin the player picked in game and writes no attribute at all. The canvas always draws the default Om Nom, so a chosen skin only shows up in a playtest.
Guide.Article.objectives.Numbering: With the **Half candy** mechanic *on*, plain candy is replaced by a left and a right half, one of each. Without it, you may place several plain candies; the editor numbers them from *0* as you place them, and rope hooks reference those numbers. The numbers are managed for you and are not shown as an editable field.
Guide.Article.objectives.Validation.Warn: Validation reports a level with no Om Nom, and a level with no candy unless a lantern is set to start with the candy captured. It also reports a candy that starts on Om Nom's mouth, because that level is won the instant it loads.
Guide.Article.stars.Title: Stars
Guide.Article.stars.Summary: Place the optional collectibles and give them a countdown.
Guide.Article.stars.InGame: Stars are the optional score objective. Collecting all three is what separates a clear from a perfect run, so they define the route you want the player to take rather than the route they must take.
Guide.Article.stars.Editing: Drag stars from the palette and place them along the arc the candy will actually travel. A star can also be given movement or spin, so it need not sit still.
Guide.Article.stars.Properties: **Duration** is the star's timeout in seconds. Leave it at *-1* for a star that waits indefinitely. A positive value makes a timed star that disappears after that many seconds, forcing the player to reach it early.
Guide.Article.stars.Timeout.Tip: Timed stars only read as fair if the player can see the clock running out. Give a timed star a wide, open approach rather than hiding it behind a puzzle.
Guide.Article.rope-hooks.Title: Rope hooks
Guide.Article.rope-hooks.Summary: The hook variants, how a rope binds to its candy, and the rail and radius handles.
Guide.Article.rope-hooks.InGame: A rope hook anchors a rope to the candy. The player cuts the rope to release it, so hooks and their lengths are the main thing shaping how the candy swings. A hook can also appear as a wheel that reels its rope in and out, a gun that shoots a rope when tapped, a suction cup that can be knocked loose, or a hook with a spider that crawls down the rope and steals the candy if it reaches it.
Guide.Article.rope-hooks.Editing: Drag a rope hook from the palette. Selecting it shows the handles for whichever variant it is: a hook with an authored rope shows a knob where its rope hangs lowest, an auto-catch hook shows a radius ring, and a hook on a rail shows the rail. Drag the knob, or the rope itself, to change the rope's length; drag the ring to resize the catch radius; drag a rail end to lengthen it; drag the hook to slide it along the rail; or drag the bar to move the whole assembly.
Guide.Article.rope-hooks.Binding: **Attach to** chooses what the rope holds. With a single candy the hook binds to it automatically. With several candies, or with the **Half candy** mechanic, pick the candy or the half you mean. You can also bind a rope to a light bulb instead of the candy. **Attach to** greys out for a gun hook and for an auto-catch hook, because neither has an authored rope: they take hold of the candy during play.
Guide.Article.rope-hooks.Rope:
**Auto rope** decides which of the next two fields you see. With it *off*, the hook has an authored rope and **Length** sets how long it starts; drag the rope or its knob on the canvas to change it.
A drag always adjusts from the length the rope already has, so touching one never rewrites it. A rope shorter than the gap to its candy draws straight whatever its length, so a plain drag will not take it below that point. **Alt-drag** does, with the length shown above the knob, and on a touchscreen use the **Length** field for that range instead.
With **Auto rope** *on*, the hook has no rope until the candy enters its **Radius**, and then it catches it.
**Movable rail** adds a track the hook slides along; **Rail length**, **Vertical rail**, and **Start offset** shape and position it.
Guide.Article.rope-hooks.Variants: **Wheel**, **Gun**, **Spider**, and **Suction cup** select the hook variant, and the editor greys out combinations the game cannot load: a hook is either a wheel or a gun, never both, and a rail cannot be combined with a wheel, a gun, a suction cup, or path movement. **Detached** starts a suction-cup hook already knocked off. **Invisible** hides the hook and its rope in game; the editor still draws it, faintly, so you can select it.
Guide.Article.rope-hooks.Bee.Note: Giving a rope hook a movement path turns it into a bee in game, and the bee leaves a pollen trail along its route. Hide pollen path suppresses that trail, and it only appears as a field once the hook is actually moving.
Guide.Article.rope-hooks.Validation.Warn:
A hook bound to a candy number that no candy has falls back to the primary candy in game, and a hook bound to a missing light bulb loses its target entirely.
Do not place a hook at exactly the same x as what its rope binds to either: the rope starts perfectly vertical, the physics has nothing to tell it which way to swing, and it picks an arbitrary direction that fights gravity. A single pixel of offset is enough.
Validation reports all three before you save or playtest.
Guide.Article.rope-hooks.Handles.Caption: A selected rope hook with radius and movable-rail handles.
Guide.Article.bubbles.Title: Bubbles
Guide.Article.bubbles.Summary: Place the lifting bubbles that carry candy upward.
Guide.Article.bubbles.InGame: A bubble captures the candy on contact and carries it steadily upward until the player taps the bubble to pop it. It is the standard way to move candy against gravity, and the pop timing is usually the puzzle.
Guide.Article.bubbles.Editing: Drag a bubble from the palette. It has no properties of its own; where it sits and what is above it is the whole design.
Guide.Article.bubbles.Hitbox.Tip: A bubble's capture area is considerably larger than it looks. Turn on **View > Show Hitboxes** before placing one near a spike or a narrow gap.
Guide.Article.air-cushions.Title: Air cushions
Guide.Article.air-cushions.Summary: Aim the pump that blows candy across the level.
Guide.Article.air-cushions.InGame: An air cushion puffs when tapped, pushing anything in front of its mouth away along the direction it faces. It is a directional shove the player triggers, so unlike a bubble it does nothing until used.
Guide.Article.air-cushions.Editing: Drag an air cushion from the palette and use its rotation dial to aim the mouth. The dial snaps in 15-degree steps when rotation snapping is on, or while you hold Alt.
Guide.Article.air-cushions.ForceField.Ti: Turn on **View > Show Force Fields** to see how far the puff actually reaches and which objects sit inside it. The reach is much longer than the artwork suggests.
Guide.Article.gravity-buttons.Title: Gravity buttons
Guide.Article.gravity-buttons.Summary: Add the switch that flips the level's gravity.
Guide.Article.gravity-buttons.InGame: Tapping a gravity button inverts gravity for the whole level, so candy that was falling starts rising. Tapping it again flips it back. Every object that responds to gravity is affected at once.
Guide.Article.gravity-buttons.Editing: Drag a gravity button from the palette. It has no properties of its own. Place it where the player can reach it without disturbing the candy's path, since they will often need it mid-swing.
Guide.Article.gravity-buttons.Single.Not: The button toggles a level-wide state rather than its own state, so placing more than one gives the player several ways to flip the same switch, not several independent gravities.
Guide.Article.bouncers.Title: Bouncers
Guide.Article.bouncers.Summary: Angle the springy surfaces that rebound the candy.
Guide.Article.bouncers.InGame: A bouncer is a springy surface that rebounds the candy on contact. The rebound follows the surface angle, so a bouncer is a way to redirect a fall into a horizontal run, or to keep candy in the air across a gap.
Guide.Article.bouncers.Editing: Drag a bouncer from the palette and aim it with its rotation dial. The palette lists one bouncer; the small and large versions are the same object with a different Size.
Guide.Article.bouncers.Properties: **Size** picks the small (*1*) or large (*2*) surface, and **Angle** is the surface orientation. A bouncer can also be given movement or spin, which makes the rebound direction change over time.
Guide.Article.bouncers.Hitbox.Note: A bouncer's collision surface is wider than its artwork and differs between the desktop and mobile physics models. Check **View > Show Hitboxes** with the model you intend the level to use.
Guide.Article.spikes.Title: Spikes
Guide.Article.spikes.Summary: Place the hazard bars and group the ones that rotate together.
Guide.Article.spikes.InGame: Spikes destroy the candy on contact and end the run. They are the level's fail state and the reason a route has to be precise. A spike can be fixed in place, or it can belong to a toggle group: pressing that group's button rotates every spike in the group at once, opening one path while closing another.
Guide.Article.spikes.Editing: Drag a spike from the palette and aim it with its rotation dial. The palette lists one spike; the four bar lengths are the same object with a different Size.
Guide.Article.spikes.Properties: **Size** picks the bar length from *1* to *4*, and **Angle** is its orientation. **Toggled** makes the spike rotatable, and **Group** is the toggle group it belongs to, so spikes sharing a group turn together. A spike can also be given movement or spin.
Guide.Article.spikes.Overlap.Warning: Validation reports a candy that starts inside a spike, because that level breaks the instant it loads. A spike's collision box is inflated beyond its artwork, so use **View > Show Hitboxes** when placing candy nearby.
Guide.Article.electric-sparks.Title: Electric sparks
Guide.Article.electric-sparks.Summary: Time the hazard that switches itself on and off.
Guide.Article.electric-sparks.InGame: An electric spark is a spike that cycles: it is harmless while off and destroys the candy while on. The player has to read the rhythm and pass through during the gap, so it turns a static hazard into a timing puzzle.
Guide.Article.electric-sparks.Editing: Drag an electric spark from the palette and aim it with its rotation dial. Its bar length is fixed and is not editable.
Guide.Article.electric-sparks.Properties: **Initial delay** is how long the spark waits, in seconds, before its first cycle; use it to stagger several sparks against each other. **On time** and **Off time** are the lengths of the dangerous and safe halves of the cycle. A spark can also be given movement or spin.
Guide.Article.electric-sparks.Timing.Tip: Two sparks with the same on and off times but different initial delays read as a chase, which is easier to time than two sparks with unrelated cycle lengths.
Guide.Article.ghosts.Title: Ghosts
Guide.Article.ghosts.Summary: Choose which objects a ghost can morph into.
Guide.Article.ghosts.InGame: A ghost is a shape-shifter. Tapping it cycles it through the states you allow, so the same spot in the level can be a bubble now and a rope hook a moment later. The cycle order is bubble, then rope hook, then bouncer, skipping any state you leave off, and idle sits between passes.
Guide.Article.ghosts.Editing: Drag a ghost from the palette. It has no rotation dial of its own; its Angle applies to the bouncer it can become.
Guide.Article.ghosts.Properties: **Auto rope**, **Bubble**, and **Bouncer** switch the three states *on* and *off*. **Radius** is the catch radius of the rope-hook state, and **Angle** is the surface angle of the bouncer state. Both are ignored while their state is *off*.
Guide.Article.ghosts.Idle.Warning: A ghost with all three states off does nothing at all in game. Validation reports it, because it is almost always an unfinished object rather than a deliberate one.
Guide.Article.magic-hats.Title: Magic hats
Guide.Article.magic-hats.Summary: Group hats into teleport pairs and aim their mouths.
Guide.Article.magic-hats.InGame: Magic hats teleport the candy. Candy that enters one hat comes out of the hat it is grouped with, keeping its speed and leaving along the direction that hat's mouth faces. A pair is therefore both a shortcut and a way to redirect a fall.
Guide.Article.magic-hats.Editing: Drag a magic hat from the palette and use its rotation dial to aim the mouth, which is where the candy leaves. The mouth sits off to one side of the hat rather than at its center.
Guide.Article.magic-hats.Grouping: **Teleport group** is what links two hats. The editor assigns it for you: a newly placed hat completes the lowest group that still has an unpaired hat, and starts a new group when every existing group is already a pair. Change it in **Properties** if you want a different pairing.
Guide.Article.magic-hats.Mouth.Note: The interactive mouth does not line up with the hat artwork, so two hats can look clear of each other while their mouths overlap. Turn on **View > Show Hitboxes** when placing a pair close together.
Guide.Article.magic-hats.Xmas.Tip: During December and January the game draws magic hats as Christmas socks. The editor's palette and canvas follow the same seasonal switch, so the artwork changing is expected, not a bug.
Guide.Article.magic-hats.Pair.Caption: A paired set of magic hats with mouth hitboxes visible.
Guide.Article.light-bulbs.Title: Light bulbs
Guide.Article.light-bulbs.Summary: Light a night level and bind ropes to a bulb instead of the candy.
Guide.Article.light-bulbs.InGame: In a night level, the stage is dimmed and the stars stay uncollectable (*idle* state) until a light bulb comes near them. Om Nom also remains asleep in this mode and cannot eat candy until he is illuminated.
Guide.Article.light-bulbs.InGame2: The bulb is a firefly in a jar that swings on its own ropes, so lighting the level is itself a rope puzzle running alongside the candy.
Guide.Article.light-bulbs.Editing: Drag a light bulb from the palette. A rope hook can be attached to a bulb instead of the candy by choosing that bulb in the hook's **Attach to** field; the editor numbers bulbs from *0* as you place them and manages those numbers for you.
Guide.Article.light-bulbs.Properties: **Lit radius** is how far the bulb's light reaches, and so how close it must pass to illuminate a star and Om Nom. Larger values make the level more forgiving.
Guide.Article.light-bulbs.NightLevel.War: Light bulbs are only meaningful with Night level turned on in Level Settings. Validation reports a night level that has no light bulb, since you can't wake Om Nom up, and the game instantly loses.
Guide.Article.lanterns.Title: Lanterns
Guide.Article.lanterns.Summary: Hold the candy in a lantern until the player releases it.
Guide.Article.lanterns.InGame: A lantern catches the candy and holds it until the player taps the lantern to release it. Lanterns share their captured candy, so a level can pass the candy from one lantern to the next and the player controls when each hand-off happens.
Guide.Article.lanterns.Editing: Drag a lantern from the palette. Place lanterns where the candy will actually arrive, since a lantern the candy never reaches does nothing.
Guide.Article.lanterns.Properties: **Starts captured** makes the level start with the candy already held in this lantern instead of loose on the stage.
Guide.Article.lanterns.NoCandy.Note: A level whose candy starts inside a lantern may legitimately contain no candy object, and validation accepts that. Without a lantern set to capture, a level with no candy is reported.
Guide.Article.vinyl.Title: Vinyl discs
Guide.Article.vinyl.Summary: Rotate a disc and everything sitting inside it.
Guide.Article.vinyl.InGame: A vinyl disc does not spin by itself. The player drags one of its handles to turn it, and every object inside the disc turns with it. Putting rope hooks, spikes, or bouncers on a disc lets the player rearrange that part of the level by hand.
Guide.Article.vinyl.Editing: Drag a vinyl disc from the palette, then place the objects you want it to carry inside its circle. Whether an object rotates with the disc is decided by whether it sits inside the disc at load time, so the disc's size and position matter more than any binding.
Guide.Article.vinyl.Properties: **Size** is the disc radius. **Handle angle** rotates the handles the player grabs, and **Single handle** removes the second handle so the disc can only be turned from one side.
Guide.Article.vinyl.Contained.Tip: Enlarging a disc silently picks up any object that ends up inside it. After resizing one, check what is now within its circle.
Guide.Article.mice.Title: Mice
Guide.Article.mice.Summary: Set the reach and timing of the mice that steal candy.
Guide.Article.mice.InGame: A mouse waits in its hole, grabs the candy when it comes within reach, carries it, and releases it somewhere else. Mice take their turn in order rather than all at once, so a row of them passes the candy along a chain.
Guide.Article.mice.Editing: Drag a mouse from the palette and use its rotation dial to aim the body; the hole itself stays upright. The activation order is shown as a label on the canvas.
Guide.Article.mice.Properties: **Radius** is how far the mouse can reach out of its hole, and **Active time** is how many seconds it stays out before retreating. **Angle** aims the body.
Guide.Article.mice.Index.Note: Mice activate in ascending index order. The editor assigns each new mouse the next unused index automatically and shows it on the canvas, so it is not an editable field.
Guide.Article.snails.Title: Snails
Guide.Article.snails.Summary: Weigh the candy down with a snail.
Guide.Article.snails.InGame: A snail latches onto the candy and drags it downward, adding weight until it is knocked off. It works against every lifting object in the level, so a bubble that would have cleared a gap no longer does. Once detached, the snail vanishes.
Guide.Article.snails.Editing: Drag a snail from the palette, in the Cut the Rope: Experiments group. It has no properties of its own; its position, and therefore whether the candy passes close enough to be caught, is the whole design.
Guide.Article.snails.Weight.Tip: Snails stack. Two snails on the same candy pull twice as hard, which is a quick way to make a lifting route deliberately impossible until the player sheds one.
Guide.Article.conveyors.Title: Conveyors
Guide.Article.conveyors.Summary: Size a belt and choose whether it runs on its own.
Guide.Article.conveyors.InGame: A conveyor carries whatever sits on it along the belt. An automatic belt runs by itself and shows an arrow for its direction; a manual belt only moves when the player drags it, which turns the belt into a control rather than a hazard.
Guide.Article.conveyors.Editing: Drag a conveyor from the palette. Selecting it exposes separate length and width handles, so the belt is resized on the canvas rather than through numbers, and a rotation dial that pivots it about its midpoint.
Guide.Article.conveyors.Properties: **Length** and **Width** are the belt's dimensions and **Angle** its orientation. **Automatic** switches between a self-running belt and a player-dragged one. For an automatic belt, **Velocity** is its speed and **Direction** is which way it runs.
Guide.Article.conveyors.Manual.Note: Velocity and Direction only apply to an automatic belt. A manual belt shows no direction arrow in game because it has no direction of its own until the player drags it.
Guide.Article.conveyors.Handles.Caption: Conveyor resize handles and rotation dial.
Guide.Article.ant-conveyors.Title: Ant conveyors
Guide.Article.ant-conveyors.Summary: Route a marching line of ants that carries objects along it.
Guide.Article.ant-conveyors.InGame: An ant conveyor is a line of ants marching along a route you draw. Anything resting on the line is carried with it, so it behaves like a conveyor that need not be straight and can bend around the level.
Guide.Article.ant-conveyors.Editing: Drag an ant conveyor from the palette, in the Cut the Rope: Experiments group. Shape its route on the canvas with the same point handles used by movement paths: drag the end nub to extend it, click a segment to insert a point, and drag a point to move it.
Guide.Article.ant-conveyors.Properties: **Path** holds the route you drew and is normally edited on the canvas rather than typed. **Move speed** is how fast the ants march, and so how fast anything riding them travels.
Guide.Article.ant-conveyors.Shape.Tip: Hold Shift while adding or dragging a point to snap the new segment's angle. A route built from clean angles is far easier to line up with the objects at either end.
Guide.Article.bamboo-tubes.Title: Bamboo tubes
Guide.Article.bamboo-tubes.Summary: Aim a tube that takes candy in one end and out the other.
Guide.Article.bamboo-tubes.InGame: A bamboo tube swallows the candy at one of its two capture openings and shoots it out of the other. In game the player can rotate the tube, so its aim at load time is a starting position rather than a fixed one.
Guide.Article.bamboo-tubes.Editing: Drag a bamboo tube from the palette, in the **Cut the Rope: Experiments** group, and set its starting aim with the rotation dial. **Angle** is its only property.
Guide.Article.bamboo-tubes.Openings.Note: A tube's two capture openings are interchangeable: candy entering either one leaves by the other. There is nothing to pair and no entrance or exit to choose.
Guide.Article.bamboo-tubes.Overlay.Capti: A bamboo tube with its rotation dial and capture openings.
Guide.Article.steam-pipes.Title: Steam pipes
Guide.Article.steam-pipes.Summary: Aim a pipe that puffs steam in bursts.
Guide.Article.steam-pipes.InGame: A steam pipe puffs steam on its own rhythm, pushing anything in the jet away from the pipe. Unlike an air cushion the player does not trigger it, so the level's timing is built around the valve rather than around a tap.
Guide.Article.steam-pipes.Editing: Drag a steam pipe from the palette and aim the jet with its rotation dial. **Angle** is its only property; the puff rhythm is fixed by the game.
Guide.Article.steam-pipes.ForceField.Tip: Turn on **View > Show Force Fields** to see the jet's reach and the marks along it. A steam pipe's push extends well past its artwork, so neighbouring objects are often inside it without looking like they are.
Guide.Article.rockets.Title: Rockets
Guide.Article.rockets.Summary: Aim a rocket and tune its thrust and burn.
Guide.Article.rockets.InGame: A rocket attaches to the candy and fires when tapped, thrusting it along the direction the rocket faces. It is the strongest push in the game, and unlike a bubble or a cushion it keeps pushing for as long as it burns.
Guide.Article.rockets.Editing: Drag a rocket from the palette, in the Cut the Rope: Experiments group, and aim it with its rotation dial.
Guide.Article.rockets.Properties: **Impulse** is the thrust strength. **Impulse factor** scales that thrust while the rope tied to the rocket is slack, so the push eases off rather than snapping. **Burn time** is how long it fires, with *-1* meaning it burns until it is spent. **Rotatable** lets the player turn the rocket during play instead of accepting your aim.
Guide.Article.rockets.Movement: A rocket also takes a **movement path**, so it can orbit a point or travel a polyline while it waits for the candy. The path stops the moment the rocket latches on, and physics takes over from there, so it only governs where the rocket is patrolling beforehand.
Guide.Article.rockets.Playtest.Tip: The editor shows placement and direction but does not simulate flight, so thrust values can only really be judged in game. Change impulse in small steps and playtest between them.
Guide.Article.rockets.Selected.Caption: A selected rocket with its direction and properties.
Guide.Article.mechanical-hands.Title: Mechanical hands
Guide.Article.mechanical-hands.Summary: Build an articulated arm segment by segment.
Guide.Article.mechanical-hands.InGame: A mechanical hand is an articulated arm with a claw that reaches out, snatches the candy, and holds it. It takes the candy away from the player rather than helping, so the shape and reach of the arm decide how much of the level is inside its grasp.
Guide.Article.mechanical-hands.Segments: The arm is edited segment by segment rather than as one object. Click a bone to select its segment, drag a joint to resize the segments either side of it, and drag the base to move the whole arm. Selecting the hand from the palette gives you a single segment to build from.
Guide.Article.mechanical-hands.Split: Hold Alt over a bone to preview a new joint at the cursor, then Alt-click to split the bone there and add a segment. To remove a segment, right-click its joint, or hover the joint and press Delete or Backspace.
Guide.Article.mechanical-hands.Propertie: **Segments** is the number of segments in the arm. It follows the splits and removals you make on the canvas, so it is normally read rather than typed.
Guide.Article.mechanical-hands.Dial.Note: A plain click on a bone only selects its segment; it never lengthens the arm. Where the claw joint overlaps the rotation dial the joint wins, so dragging there resizes the segment instead of rotating it.
Mechanical-hand bones, joints, selected segment, and Alt split preview.
Guide.Article.motion.Title: Movement paths and spin
Guide.Article.motion.Summary: Make objects travel a route or turn in place.
Guide.Article.motion.Paths.Heading: Movement paths
Guide.Article.motion.Modes: An object that supports movement can orbit a point or follow a polyline. Orbit takes a radius, a speed, and a direction. A polyline takes the route you draw plus a speed, an option to retrace it back and forth instead of jumping to the start, and an option to close it into a loop.
Guide.Article.motion.Edit.Steps:
Select a moving object and choose Orbit or Polyline in Properties.
For an orbit, drag the circle itself to resize its radius.
For a polyline, drag the end nub to extend the route, or click a segment to insert a point.
Drag any point to reshape the route.
To remove a point, right-click it, or hover it and press Delete or Backspace. The starting anchor cannot be removed.
Guide.Article.motion.Angles.Tip: Hold Shift while adding or dragging a point to constrain that segment to a snapped angle.
Guide.Article.motion.Limit.Note: A polyline holds up to 99 points, and the editor shows a hint when a path reaches the limit. **View > Show Movement Paths** draws every path in the level, including those whose objects are not selected. Switching it off also takes away the orbit circle, so the ring cannot be dragged while paths are hidden.
Guide.Article.motion.Spin.Heading: Spin
Guide.Article.motion.Spin: **Spin** turns an object in place, independently of any path it follows. Stars, spikes, electric sparks, magic hats, and bouncers support it. Switch on **Spin object**, then set the speed and whether it turns clockwise. Spinning a spike or a spark sweeps its hazard through an arc, which is a different puzzle from moving it along a path.
Guide.Article.motion.Polyline.Caption: Editing a polyline path and its points.
Guide.Article.tutorial-objects.Title: Tutorial icons and text
Guide.Article.tutorial-objects.Summary: Add on-screen hints with gesture icons and wrapped text.
Guide.Article.tutorial-objects.InGame: Tutorial icons and text are the level's own instructions, drawn on the stage to show a new player what to do. They have no physics and nothing interacts with them.
Guide.Article.tutorial-objects.Icons: The palette lists one tutorial icon; the eleven artworks, from a cut line to arrows, a pop, a warning, and a pair of fingers, are the same object with a different **Icon**. Each icon also has an **Angle**, so a pointing arrow can be aimed.
Guide.Article.tutorial-objects.Text: Tutorial text starts in auto-width mode, so its box grows with what you type. Dragging its width handle switches it to a fixed wrap width and the text wraps within it; the height always follows the content.
Guide.Article.tutorial-objects.Editing: Select a tutorial text and press **F2** to edit it in place on the canvas. **Enter** accepts the edit and **Shift-Enter** inserts a line break. Use the **tutorial language picker** above the canvas to view one localized variant at a time.
New tutorial objects are authored in English, and the game only shows a tutorial when the player's language matches the variant. Text left in a language the player is not using simply will not appear.
Guide.Article.tutorial-objects.Width.Cap: Tutorial icon and editable tutorial text width.
Guide.Article.object-reference.Title: Object reference
Guide.Article.object-reference.Summary: A one-line index of every palette object and where its article is.
Guide.Article.object-reference.Intro: Every object below has its own article in the Objects section, covering what it does in game, how it is edited, and each of its properties. This page is the index.
Guide.Article.object-reference.Goals: Om Nom is the target and candy is the objective; half-candy levels use a left and a right half instead of one candy. Stars are the optional score objective and can be given a countdown.
Guide.Article.object-reference.Forces: Bubbles lift candy, air cushions puff it away when tapped, steam pipes puff on their own rhythm, bouncers rebound it, gravity buttons flip the level's gravity, and conveyors carry whatever rests on them.
Guide.Article.object-reference.Hazards: Spikes destroy the candy on contact and can be grouped so a button rotates them together. Electric sparks are spikes that cycle between safe and dangerous on a timer.
Guide.Article.object-reference.Night: Light bulbs illuminate idle stars in a night level and can have ropes tied to them instead of to the candy. In this mode, losing the light bulb triggers game loss, much like losing the candy.
Guide.Article.object-reference.Transport: Rope hooks anchor the ropes the player cuts. Magic hats teleport candy between grouped pairs. Vinyl discs rotate cetain things sitting inside them when the player drags a handle. Mice steal and carry it in turn. Lanterns catch the candy and hold it until the player lets it go. Conveyors move certain objects around. Ghosts morph between a bubble, a rope hook, and a bouncer as the player taps them.
Guide.Article.object-reference.Experimen: Rockets thrust the candy when fired, mechanical hands reach out and snatch it, snails latch on and weigh it down, ant conveyors march it along a drawn route, and bamboo tubes swallow it at one opening and eject it from the other.
Guide.Article.object-reference.Details.N: The palette groups objects by the game they come from. Select any placed object to see the exact fields this editor supports for it; fields whose meaning is not obvious carry an inline help button.
Guide.Article.menus-commands.Title: Menus and commands
Guide.Article.menus-commands.Summary: Find file, editing, viewing, and help commands.
Guide.Article.menus-commands.File: **New**, **Open**, **Save**, and **Save As**; **Play This Level** and **Set DX Location** for playtesting; **Screenshot** to export a PNG; **Review Changes** to inspect the XML diff; and **Close**.
Guide.Article.menus-commands.Edit: **Undo** and **Redo**, clipboard and selection commands, grid and rotation snapping, and **Level Settings**.
Guide.Article.menus-commands.View: **Zoom In**, **Zoom Out**, and **Zoom to Fit**; **Play Animations** and **Stop Animations**; and the **Show Hitboxes**, **Show Force Fields**, and **Show Movement Paths** overlays.
Guide.Article.menus-commands.Help: Open this **Usage Guide**. **About** is also here on Windows, Linux, and the browser; macOS keeps **About** in the application menu.
Guide.Article.keyboard-shortcuts.Title: Keyboard shortcuts
Guide.Article.keyboard-shortcuts.Summary: Use the editor's global file, editing, preview, and zoom commands.
Guide.Article.keyboard-shortcuts.SearchT: ctrl shift p|command shift p|hotkeys|keys|space|delete|f2|tutorial text
Guide.Article.keyboard-shortcuts.Platfor: Use Command instead of Ctrl on macOS. Ctrl/Command-Shift-Z is redo everywhere; Ctrl-Y is an extra redo binding on Windows and Linux only. These chords are ignored while a dialog is open, so the dialog's own text fields keep them.
Guide.Article.keyboard-shortcuts.Shortcu: Ctrl/⌘ Shift Z, or Ctrl Y
Remove hovered path point or hand joint
Guide.Article.pointer-gestures.Title: Pointer, trackpad, and touch gestures
Guide.Article.pointer-gestures.Summary: Navigate and edit with a mouse, trackpad, touchscreen, or pen.
Guide.Article.pointer-gestures.Mouse: Drag empty canvas space or **middle-drag** to pan. The wheel scrolls, and **Shift-wheel** turns a vertical wheel into horizontal scrolling. **Ctrl-wheel** zooms around the pointer, on *every platform* including macOS.
Guide.Article.pointer-gestures.Touch: Trackpad magnify and touchscreen pinch gestures zoom around their origin. Touch uses a larger drag threshold than a mouse, so a slightly unsteady tap still registers as a tap. Compact layouts add explicit **Edit** and **Pan** interaction modes.
Guide.Article.pointer-gestures.Context: **Right-click** removes a polyline point or a mechanical-hand joint; hovering one and pressing **Delete** or **Backspace** does the same. **Double-click** an object to lock or unlock it.
Guide.Article.pointer-gestures.Locked.No: While an object is locked, it is the only thing the canvas responds to: clicks never fall through to objects underneath it. Double-click it again to unlock, or use the lock button on its row in Layers.
Guide.Article.modifier-keys.Title: Modifier keys
Guide.Article.modifier-keys.Summary: Learn when Command, Ctrl, Shift, and Alt change an editing gesture.
Guide.Article.modifier-keys.Shortcut.Sel: Add or remove an object from the selection
Guide.Article.modifier-keys.Shortcut.Dup: Duplicate the selection while moving it
Guide.Article.modifier-keys.Shortcut.Hor: Scroll horizontally with a vertical wheel
Guide.Article.modifier-keys.Option.Note: Ctrl and Command are interchangeable for selecting and duplicating, on every platform. On macOS the Alt key is labelled Option. Ctrl-wheel zoom is Ctrl everywhere, including macOS.
Guide.Article.snapping.Title: Snapping and precision editing
Guide.Article.snapping.Toggles: **Edit > Snap to Grid** controls positional snapping while placing and dragging objects. **Edit > Snap Rotation** keeps rotation dials on *15-degree* steps.
Guide.Article.snapping.Temporary: Hold **Alt** during a rotation drag to snap just that drag, without changing the toggle. Hold **Shift** while adding or dragging a path point to constrain that segment's angle.
Guide.Article.snapping.Properties.Tip: Canvas handles and Properties fields edit the same values, so follow a visual placement with Properties whenever a coordinate, angle, length, or radius has to be exact.
Guide.Article.animation-preview.Title: Animation preview
Guide.Article.animation-preview.Summary: Preview animated sprites for one object or the whole level.
Guide.Article.animation-preview.Usage: Choose **View > Start animation preview** or press **Space** to preview supported animations throughout the level. Use the play control on an object row to preview only that object.
Guide.Article.animation-preview.Scope.No: Animation preview shows visual animation, not complete game physics or object interactions.
Guide.Article.diagnostic-overlays.Title: Diagnostic overlays
Guide.Article.diagnostic-overlays.Summar: Inspect collision boxes, force reach, and movement routes.
Guide.Article.diagnostic-overlays.Hitbox: **View > Show Hitboxes** draws the collision boxes the game actually tests, which are often quite different from the artwork. Candy, stars, Om Nom, bubbles, spikes, electric sparks, bouncers, rockets, snails, and magic-hat mouths all have one. The boxes follow the level's physics model, so turning **Use mobile physics** *on* or *off* in **Level Settings** changes what you see.
Guide.Article.diagnostic-overlays.ForceF: **View > Show Force Fields** draws the reach and direction of the two directional emitters, air cushions and steam pipes, with marks along the jet. Both push much further than their artwork suggests.
Guide.Article.diagnostic-overlays.Paths: **View > Show Movement Paths** draws every movement route in the level at once, including those belonging to objects that are not selected. It is the quickest way to see two moving objects that will collide.
Guide.Article.diagnostic-overlays.Editor: Overlays are editor-only diagnostics. They are never written into the level file and never become gameplay objects.
Guide.Article.diagnostic-overlays.Enable: A level with all three diagnostic overlays enabled.
Guide.Article.validation-review.Title: Validate and review changes
Guide.Article.validation-review.Summary: Catch likely gameplay problems and inspect the XML changes before saving.
Guide.Article.validation-review.SearchTe: validator|warning|review changes|diff|missing candy|missing om nom|unplayable|physics|vertical rope
Guide.Article.validation-review.Validati: Before a save or a playtest, the editor checks the level for states that make it crash or play incorrectly in Cut the Rope: DX, and lists whatever it finds.
Guide.Article.validation-review.Checks.S:
No Om Nom, or no candy and no lantern set to capture it.
A half-candy level missing a half, or still containing a plain candy; a normal level containing halves.
A night level with no light bulb.
A rope hook bound to a candy number no candy has, or to a light bulb that is not there.
A rope hook sitting at exactly the same x as what its rope binds to, which confuses the physics engine.
Two candies sharing a number, which hooks cannot tell apart.
A ghost with none of its three states enabled, which will sit idle.
Candy starting inside a spike, or starting on Om Nom's mouth.
A resolution below 320x480, or more than one settings layer.
Guide.Article.validation-review.Review: **File > Review Changes** compares the live document against the version you last opened or saved. Choose the *split* or *unified* view and step through what was added, removed, and modified.
Guide.Article.validation-review.Warnings: These are warnings, not refusals, and nothing is discarded. After reading them you can go back and edit, or continue with Save anyway, Edit anyway, or Play Anyway.
The validation prompt and Review Changes dialog.
Guide.Article.save-export-playtest.Title: Save, export, and playtest
Guide.Article.save-export-playtest.Summa: Save XML, export a rendered image, and launch the level in Cut the Rope: DX.
Guide.Article.save-export-playtest.Save: **Save** writes to the current file when the platform supports it; **Save As** chooses a new destination. **Screenshot** exports the rendered level as a PNG.
Guide.Article.save-export-playtest.Playt: On desktop, point the editor at the game once with **File > Set DX Location**, then use **File > Play This Level**. The editor validates the level and writes a temporary playtest copy before launching, so you can try unsaved work.
Guide.Article.save-export-playtest.Brows: The browser cannot launch a local game executable. This is by design to minimize security risks. Download or save the level, then open it with your desktop workflow.
Guide.Article.troubleshooting.Title: Troubleshooting
Guide.Article.troubleshooting.Summary: Resolve missing assets, disabled objects, unexpected selection, and playtest problems.
Guide.Article.troubleshooting.SearchTerm: assets required|disabled palette|cannot select|playtest error|locked layer|greyed out|no rope
Guide.Article.troubleshooting.Palette.He: An object is disabled in the palette
Guide.Article.troubleshooting.Palette: Check the mechanics in **Edit > Level Settings**. Plain candy is disabled while **Half candy** is *on*, and the left and right halves are disabled while it is *off*. A level already holding the maximum number of an object also disables it.
Guide.Article.troubleshooting.Selection: Check the object and its parent layer for a hidden or locked state in **Layers**; a locked or hidden parent layer applies to its objects even when the object's own row looks enabled. If some other object is locked, it captures every click until you unlock it. Where objects overlap, clicking repeatedly cycles through the ones under the cursor.
Guide.Article.troubleshooting.Rope.Headi: A rope hook shows no rope
Guide.Article.troubleshooting.Rope: A hook with **Auto rope** *on* has no rope until the candy enters its radius, and a **Gun** hook has none until the player fires it. Both are correct. If you wanted an authored rope, turn **Auto rope** *off* and set a **Length**.
Guide.Article.troubleshooting.Playtest: Use **File > Set DX Location** again and confirm the application or executable you chose still exists and is runnable. On Linux and macOS a development build may also need to be marked executable.
Guide.Article.troubleshooting.Assets: Complete the guided asset setup by downloading supported assets or choosing a valid asset zip.

Dialog.LevelSettings.ResolutionDescripti: Sets the level's width and height in game units. Choose Custom to enter a size that is not in the preset list.
Dialog.LevelSettings.RopePhysicsSpeedDes: Controls how quickly rope physics are simulated. 1 is the normal speed; higher positive values make ropes react faster.
Dialog.LevelSettings.GravityDescription:

Dialog.LevelSettings.MobilePhysicsDescri: Use the mobile physics model (writes useMobilePhysics to the level's gameDesign).

Attr.impulse.Help: Thrust strength determines how hard the rocket pushes the attached candy while firing. Higher values launch it faster and farther; 0 means no thrust.
Attr.impulseFactor.Help: Slack-rope thrust multiplier. While the rope tied to the rocket is loose, its thrust is scaled by this factor so the push eases off. Default 0.6; 1 keeps full thrust when slack, lower is gentler.
Attr.time.Help: How many seconds the rocket burns once fired. -1 lets it burn until it is spent; a positive value cuts the thrust short after that many seconds.
Attr.isRotatable.Help: Lets the player turn the rocket during play instead of accepting the angle you set. Off means your aim is final.
Attr.timeout.Help: How many seconds the star waits before disappearing. -1 keeps it on screen indefinitely; a positive value makes a timed star the player has to reach early.
Attr.attachTo.Help: Which object this hook's rope holds. With a single candy it binds automatically. Choose a specific candy, a candy half, or a light bulb when the level has more than one possible target. Greyed out for a gun or auto-rope hook, because neither has an authored rope: they take hold of the candy during play.
Attr.autoCatch.Help: Off gives the hook a rope from the start, with its length set below. On removes that rope and makes the hook catch the candy whenever it comes within the radius set below.
Attr.length.Help: How long this object is: a rope hook's starting rope, or a conveyor belt's span. Shorter ropes swing faster and reach less far.
Attr.radius.Help: How far this object reaches, drawn as a ring on the canvas: the distance at which an auto-rope hook or a ghost's hook state catches the candy, or how far a mouse can stretch out of its hole.
Attr.movable.Help: Puts the hook on a rail it slides along during play, instead of fixing it in one spot. Cannot be combined with a wheel, a gun, a suction cup, or path movement.
Attr.moveLength.Help: How long the rail is. Drag the rail's end on the canvas to change it visually.
Attr.moveVertical.Help: Runs the rail up and down instead of side to side.
Attr.moveOffset.Help: Where along the rail the hook starts, measured from the rail's first end. 0 starts it at that end.
Attr.wheel.Help: Makes the hook a wheel that reels its rope in and out as the player drags it. A hook is either a wheel or a gun, never both.
Attr.gun.Help: Makes the hook a gun that shoots a rope at the candy when tapped, rather than starting with one attached.
Attr.spider.Help: Puts a spider on the hook's rope. It crawls down toward the candy during play and steals it if it arrives, so the player has to cut that rope in time.
Attr.kickable.Help: Makes the hook a suction cup that can be knocked loose by the candy, dropping its rope.
Attr.kicked.Help: Starts a suction-cup hook already knocked loose, so its rope is detached when the level begins.
Attr.invisible.Help: Hides the hook and its rope in game. The editor still draws it, faintly, so you can select and move it.
Attr.hidePath.Help: A hook with a movement path becomes a bee in game and leaves a pollen trail along its route. This hides that trail.
Attr.grab.Help: Lets the ghost morph into a rope hook, using the radius below. Tapping the ghost cycles through whichever states are enabled.
Attr.bubble.Help: Lets the ghost morph into a bubble that lifts the candy.
Attr.bouncer.Help: Lets the ghost morph into a bouncer, using the angle below.
Attr.litRadius.Help: How far the bulb's light reaches, and so how close it has to pass for an idle star to be revealed. Larger values make a night level more forgiving.
Attr.candyCaptured.Help: Starts the level with the candy already held inside this lantern instead of loose on the stage. A level whose candy starts captured needs no separate candy object.
Attr.sockGroup.Help: Links two magic hats into a teleport pair: candy entering one leaves from the other. The editor fills open pairs before starting a new group, so this is normally set for you.
Attr.toggled.Help: Makes the spike rotatable rather than fixed, so a button can turn it during play. The group below decides which button controls it.
Attr.toggleGroup.Help: Which toggle group the spike belongs to. Every spike sharing a group rotates together when that group's button is pressed.
Attr.initialDelay.Help: How many seconds this spark waits before its first cycle. Give several sparks different delays to stagger them against each other.
Attr.onTime.Help: How many seconds the spark stays on, destroying any candy that touches it.
Attr.offTime.Help: How many seconds the spark stays off, leaving a safe gap for the candy to pass through.
Attr.handleAngle.Help: Rotates the handles the player grabs to turn the disc. It does not rotate the disc's contents.
Attr.oneHandle.Help: Removes the second handle, so the disc can only be turned from one side.
Attr.activeTime.Help: How many seconds the mouse stays out of its hole before retreating, whether or not it caught the candy.
Attr.auto.Help: On makes the belt run by itself, using the velocity and direction below, and shows a direction arrow in game. Off makes it a manual belt that only moves while the player drags it.
Attr.velocity.Help: How fast an automatic belt carries whatever rests on it. Ignored by a manual belt.
Attr.moveSpeed.Help: How fast this object travels along its route. For an ant conveyor it is the marching speed of the ants, and so the speed of anything riding them.
Attr.segmentsCount.Help: How many segments the arm has. This follows the splits and removals you make on the canvas, so it is normally read rather than typed.
Attr.spin.Help: Turns the object in place, independently of any movement path it follows.
Attr.spinSpeed.Help: How fast the object turns in place. Higher values spin faster.
Attr.spinClockwise.Help: Turns the object clockwise; off turns it counter-clockwise.
Attr.movementMode.Help: None keeps the object still. Orbit circles it around its position using the radius and speed below. Polyline follows a route you draw on the canvas.
Attr.orbitRadius.Help: How far the object sits from the centre of its orbit.
Attr.orbitSpeed.Help: How fast the object travels around its orbit.
Attr.polylineSpeed.Help: How fast the object travels along its drawn route.
Attr.polylineRetrace.Help: Retraces the route backwards on reaching the end, instead of jumping back to the start.
Attr.closedLoop.Help: Joins the route's last point back to its first, so the object circles continuously.
Attr.path.Help: The route this object follows, stored as a list of points. Shape it on the canvas rather than typing it: drag the end nub to extend it, click a segment to insert a point, and drag a point to move it.
Attr.width.Help: How wide this object is: a conveyor belt's thickness, or a tutorial text's wrap width. Dragging a tutorial text's width handle switches it out of auto-width mode and sets this; its height always follows the content.
Attr.targetType.Help: Which Om Nom skin this level forces. Player's choice leaves the skin to whatever the player picked in game, and writes no targetType attribute.
Hint.PolylinePointLimit: Movement path is at its 99-point limit
Validation.TwoPartMissingHalf: Two-part level is missing a candy half.
Validation.TwoPartHasPlainCandy: Two-part level shouldn't contain a plain candy.
Validation.NightNoBulb: Night level has no light bulb.
Validation.DuplicateSettingsLayer: Multiple settings layers found; only the first one is used.
Validation.DuplicateCandyNumber: Duplicate candyNumber values found; grabs cannot tell those candies apart.
Validation.GrabUnmatchedCandyNumber: A grab references candyNumber '{0}', which no candy has, it will bind to the primary candy.
Validation.GrabUnmatchedBulbNumber: A grab binds to bulbNumber '{0}', which no light bulb has.
Validation.GrabVerticallyAligned: A grab and what its rope binds to are both at x={0}. Offset one of them by a pixel or more.
Validation.GhostIdle: A ghost has no enabled states (grab/bubble/bouncer), it will sit idle and do nothing.
Validation.CandyInHazard: Candy {0} starts inside a spike and will break immediately.
Validation.CandyOnMouth: Candy {0} starts on Om Nom's mouth and will be eaten immediately, winning the level.
Validation.RocketWithoutMobilePhysics: Level has a rocket but mobile physics is off; rockets are tuned for mobile physics and will feel off without it.
Validation.WaterWithoutMobilePhysics: Level has water but mobile physics is off; water is tuned for mobile physics and will feel off without it.
Validation.SnailWithoutMobilePhysics: Level has a snail but mobile physics is off; snails are tuned for mobile physics and will feel off without it.
